title: Human Factors in Patient Safety
path: Quality Improvement in Healthcare and Patient Safety

headings.title: Introduction to Human Factors and Ergonomics
headings.content: Human factors science looks at how people interact with the tools, tasks, environments, and other people around them. In nursing, this means designing systems that fit human strengths and protect against human limitations. When a medication error happens, blaming the individual nurse rarely fixes the root problem. Instead, human factors looks deeper to see if confusing pump dials, poor lighting, or rushed shift handovers set that nurse up to fail. Ergonomics focuses heavily on matching the physical and mental demands of clinical work to the actual capacity of healthcare workers.

headings.title: The Swiss Cheese Model of System Accidents
headings.content:
James Reason's Swiss Cheese Model explains that major accidents in healthcare rarely happen because of one single failure. Instead, they occur when multiple small breakdowns in safety line up all at once. Think of defenses in a hospital as slices of Swiss cheese, where each slice has holes representing weaknesses. These holes are constantly moving and changing size.

- **Active failures**: Unsafe acts committed directly by workers in contact with the patient, such as misreading a dose.
- **Latent conditions**: Hidden flaws built into the system long before, such as chronic understaffing, broken equipment, or confusing drug packaging.

An adverse event only occurs when the holes in every single layer of cheese temporarily line up, allowing a hazard to pass straight through to harm the patient.

headings.title: Cognitive Biases and Mental Workload in Nursing
headings.content: Nurses process massive amounts of information under intense pressure every day. Working memory has strict limits, and when mental workload gets too high, shortcuts known as heuristics take over. While these mental shortcuts save time, they also open the door to cognitive biases. Confirmation bias, for instance, leads a nurse to notice signs that support their initial impression of a patient while ignoring contradictory vital signs. Tunnel vision can set in during an emergency, causing the team to miss obvious secondary clues because all attention is locked onto a single crisis.

headings.title: Fatigue, Shift Work, and Vigilance
headings.content: Human alertness is governed by circadian rhythms that make night shifts biologically punishing. Chronic sleep deprivation impairs reaction time, problem-solving, and mood just as severely as alcohol intoxication. Vigilance naturally drops during long, monotonous tasks, making it dangerously easy to miss subtle changes in a monitor or intravenous infusion. A tired nurse is far more likely to experience lapses in attention during high-risk tasks like medication calculation. Managing fatigue requires more than telling staff to sleep; it demands sensible roster planning, protected break times, and manageable shift lengths.

headings.title: Communication and Teamwork Human Factors
headings.content: Breakdowns in communication remain one of the leading root causes of sentinel events in hospitals. Traditional medical hierarchies can intimidate junior nurses from speaking up when they notice a dangerous prescription or a worsening patient condition. Standardized communication tools like SBAR (Situation, Background, Assessment, Recommendation) level the playing field by giving everyone a clear, predictable script to share critical data. Active listening, closed-loop communication where instructions are repeated back, and mutual respect build a resilient team culture where safety concerns can be raised without fear of ridicule.

headings.title: Designing Systems to Prevent Human Error
headings.content: Because humans will inevitably make mistakes, healthcare systems must be engineered with fault-tolerant designs. For instance, forcing functions make it physically impossible to perform a dangerous action, such as enteral feeding tubes that will not connect to intravenous lines. Standardization ensures that identical equipment across different wards operates the same way, reducing confusion during emergencies. Redundancy adds double-checks for high-risk processes, such as two nurses independently verifying high-alert medications like insulin before administration.

headings.title: Applying Human Factors in Nigerian Clinical Settings
headings.content: Applying human factors principles in Nigerian healthcare requires navigating unique local challenges alongside universal safety goals. Resource-constrained environments often mean nurses face severe staff shortages, frequent power outages, and poorly maintained equipment, which drastically increases mental workload and fatigue. Designing safe systems under these conditions involves making the best use of local workarounds while advocating for structural improvements. Simple changes—such as color-coding emergency trolley drawers, standardizing drug dilution charts at the nursing station, and implementing peer-led safety briefings—can protect patients even when high-tech solutions are unavailable.
